About: Radioactive Decay — a Law With No Schedule

Source

Topic
Nuclear physics — radioactive decay (JEE / NCERT Class 12)
Concept
Decay is a memoryless statistical law: each nucleus has the same chance of decaying every second, regardless of history.
Serves
Distinguishing mean lifetime τ from half-life T½ = τ ln 2; recognising the exponential as an emergent property of many independent random draws.
Inquiry
If you drop the starting count from 2500 to 50, does the curve get smoother, stay the same, or get rougher?
Misconception
"A long-lived nucleus is 'due' to decay soon" and "half-life means the rest is stable." Both are wrong — the process is memoryless and every further half-life removes half of whatever remains.

Guided Inquiry

1. Watch a large sample decay

The left panel shows a few thousand nuclei. Each one is independent: every second, it has the same fixed chance of decaying — no ageing, no schedule.

The run starts on its own — watch dots wink out at random on the left, and the surviving count trace a smooth curve on the right.

Half-life markers (T½, 2T½, 3T½ …) stand on the time axis. The curve should cross each at half the previous value.

2. Predict — drop N₀ from 2500 to 50

If you start with only 50 nuclei instead of 2500, the curve will be:

3. Set N₀ = 50 and observe

Drag the Initial count N₀ slider all the way down. The right panel will still try to draw a curve — but now it staircases visibly.

Each downward step is one nucleus decaying. That is the raw physical event; the smooth exponential you saw before was the crowd average.

Reset and re-run at N₀ = 50 a few times. Each run is a different staircase — but they all cluster around the same exponential.

4. Mean lifetime vs half-life

After one mean lifetime τ, what fraction survives?

5. The one thing to notice

No nucleus is ageing or counting down. Each has the same chance every second, forever — a memoryless process.

The smooth exponential on the right is just what a crowd of independent coin flips looks like. Every further half-life removes another half of whatever remains — a quarter, an eighth, a sixteenth… never zero.

Free-play: change τ and N₀ freely. Watch how the curve refits to the new half-life, and how small samples turn ragged.

The Physics

Radioactive Decay — a Law With No Schedule · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A sample of identical unstable nuclei, one dot each, decays over time. The left panel shows each nucleus. The right panel plots the fraction that is left.

What you'll learn

  • What a mean lifetime τ and a half-life T½ each measure.
  • How the chance of a single decay becomes a rule for a whole sample.
  • How the starting count N₀ shapes what you see.
Before the run starts, every nucleus is intact and the plot is empty.

What's on screen

  • Bright dot: a nucleus that has not decayed.
  • Small grey dot: a nucleus that has decayed.
  • Teal trace: the fraction N/N₀ left, drawn as the run goes.
  • Dashed curve and T½ marks: the theory curve, with a vertical line at each half-life.
See itLet the default run play from the start. Watch for: dots dimming one by one at random places in the grid, while the teal trace starts to fall.

03

Every nucleus has the same chance of decaying each second

Radioactive decay is random for each nucleus and has no schedule. A nucleus does not age or count down. One that has lasted a minute is exactly as likely to go in the next second as a new one. This is a memoryless process.

The chance per second is the decay constant λ, and it is the reciprocal of the mean lifetime:

λ = 1 / τ
The sim lets each surviving nucleus decay in a time step dt with probability 1 − e−dt/τ.

The number of decays each second is the activity A = λN, measured in becquerel (1 decay per second = 1 Bq). Fewer nuclei means fewer decays per second.

τ (s)1020100400
λ (s⁻¹)0.10000.05000.01000.0025
A at N = 2500 (Bq)250125256.25
See itUse τ = 20 s and N₀ = 2500, and watch the Live Readouts. Watch for: λ = 0.0500 s⁻¹ and an activity near 100 decays/s, which keeps falling as dots go dim.
04

After one mean lifetime about 37% of the nuclei remain

A constant chance per second makes the count fall exponentially:

N(t) / N0 = e−t/τ = e−λt
At t = τ the fraction left is 1/e ≈ 0.368, not one half.

The half-life T½ is the time to lose half. Setting e−t/τ = ½ gives T½ = τ ln 2 ≈ 0.693 τ. It is shorter than τ. Each further half-life halves what is left: after n half-lives the fraction is (½)n.

t / τ0.693123
N / N₀0.5000.3680.1350.050
See itUse τ = 10 s with N₀ = 5000 and let the run finish. Watch for: the amber 1/e ≈ 0.37 line, crossed at τ = 10 s, later than the T½ = 6.9 s mark.
05

A small sample decays in visible steps around the same curve

The smooth exponential is the average over a crowd of independent coin flips. It is not a schedule that each nucleus follows. With only a few nuclei the count of survivors scatters from run to run, because the number lost in a short time is itself random.

At t = T½ the expected survivors are N₀/2, and the typical scatter is about ½√N₀ nuclei. As a fraction of N₀ that is 0.5/√N₀. With N₀ = 2500 this is 1%, and with N₀ = 50 it is 7%.

Each decay of a 50-nucleus sample drops the plot by 1/50 = 0.02, a step you can see. A 2500-nucleus sample drops it by 0.0004, too small to see. A repeat of the same run gives a different staircase, and every one stays near the same dashed curve.

See itSet N₀ = 50 with τ = 20 s. Watch for: single steps down in the teal trace, as one dot at a time goes dim.
06

Where it matters

  • Radiocarbon dating. Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5730 years. The fraction left in a sample gives its age.
  • Medical tracers. Technetium-99m has a half-life of about 6 hours. After a day only about 6% of it is left, so the patient's dose falls quickly.
  • Identifying an isotope. Each radioactive isotope has its own half-life, so how fast a sample's activity falls helps tell what it is.
  • Radioactive waste. How long a waste needs storing is set by its half-life, because each half-life only halves the activity and never clears it entirely.
07

Summary

In one line. Each nucleus has a fixed chance of decaying every second, and a whole sample follows from that.

Key points

  • The decay constant is λ = 1/τ, and the activity is A = λN.
  • N/N₀ = e−t/τ, so 1/e ≈ 0.368 is left at t = τ.
  • T½ = τ ln 2 ≈ 0.693 τ, and each half-life halves the count.
  • Small samples are ragged, and large ones are smooth.

Common mix-ups

  • "After one mean lifetime, half is gone." Half is gone after T½ = 0.693 τ. At τ, 37% is left.
  • "A nucleus that has lasted a long time is due to decay." The chance per second never changes.
  • "After two half-lives, nothing is left." A quarter is left, and the count never reaches zero in theory.

Things to try on your own

  • Predict the fraction left at t = 2τ, then read it from the plot.
  • Run N₀ = 50 five times and compare the staircases.
